title: Heredity: Classical and Molecular Genetics
summary: Heredity is scored on work you can show. Nearly every station ends in a number or a diagram you have to produce — a ratio from a cross, a carrier probability from a pedigree, an allele frequency from a population, a protein change from one swapped base — so the molecular half is taught as the machinery that explains those results, not as vocabulary.
objectives: Work monohybrid, dihybrid and test crosses to stated genotypic and phenotypic ratios, and use probability rules where a grid would be slower.
Read a pedigree for dominant versus recessive and autosomal versus sex-linked, and compute the probability that a named individual is a carrier.
Account for the results Mendel's two laws do not predict: linkage and recombination, incomplete dominance, codominance, complementation and recessive epistasis.
Compare mitosis with meiosis stage by stage, and read a human karyotype for nondisjunction, aneuploidy and structural rearrangement.
Trace a gene from DNA sequence through replication, transcription, RNA processing and translation, and give the protein-level consequence of a substitution, insertion or deletion.
Compute Hardy–Weinberg allele and genotype frequencies, and name the violated assumption behind an observed change.

units.title: Mendel's Laws and the Monohybrid Cross
units.summary: Mendel's results are the only part of this event a student can rederive from first principles; everything later in the season is a departure from them and has to be recognised as one.
objectives: State the law of segregation and the law of independent assortment in terms of alleles and gametes.
Work a monohybrid cross or a test cross through to genotypic and phenotypic ratios.

lessons.title: Segregation and Independent Assortment
lessons.objective: State the law of segregation and the law of independent assortment, and identify which observed cross result each one predicts.

lessons.title: Monohybrid Crosses and Punnett Squares
lessons.objective: Build a Punnett square for a monohybrid cross and report both ratios, including the 3:1 phenotypic and 1:2:1 genotypic results.

lessons.title: Test Crosses: Finding a Hidden Genotype
lessons.objective: Given an individual showing a dominant phenotype, set up a test cross and decide its genotype from the offspring ratio.

units.title: Two Genes at Once, and the Arithmetic That Beats a Grid
units.summary: A 16-box square is slow and error-prone under time; the same answers fall out of the product and sum rules in a fraction of the time, and three-gene questions leave no alternative.
objectives: Work a dihybrid cross to the 9:3:3:1 ratio and explain where it comes from.
Compute an offspring probability using the product rule and the sum rule instead of a grid.

lessons.title: Dihybrid Crosses and 9:3:3:1
lessons.objective: Enumerate the four gamete types from a dihybrid parent and work the cross to the 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio.

lessons.title: Product Rule, Sum Rule and the Forked Line
lessons.objective: Compute the probability of a specified offspring genotype by multiplying independent single-gene probabilities and adding mutually exclusive outcomes, without drawing the full square.

units.title: Where Mendel's Ratios Break
units.summary: State and national papers are built on the exceptions: a ratio that is not 3:1 or 9:3:3:1 is the question, and the job is to name which departure produced it.
objectives: Identify incomplete dominance, codominance and multiple-allele systems from heterozygote phenotypes.
Compute recombination frequency from offspring counts and read a modified dihybrid ratio as epistasis.

lessons.title: Incomplete Dominance, Codominance and Multiple Alleles
lessons.objective: Classify a heterozygote phenotype as incomplete dominance or codominance, and predict ABO blood types from parental genotypes.

lessons.title: Recessive Epistasis and the Complementation Test
lessons.objective: Recognise recessive epistasis from a modified dihybrid ratio, and read a complementation test as same-gene or different-gene mutations.

lessons.title: Linked Genes, Crossing Over and Map Distance
lessons.objective: Compute recombination frequency from recombinant and parental offspring counts and convert it to map distance in centimorgans.

units.title: Pedigrees
units.summary: A pedigree is a data set, not a family tree: the symbols are fixed, the inheritance pattern is deduced from skipped generations and affected sexes, and the answer is usually a probability.
objectives: Construct a pedigree from a family description using standard symbols.
Deduce the inheritance pattern and compute a carrier probability for a named individual.

lessons.title: Reading and Building a Pedigree
lessons.objective: Construct a pedigree from a family description using standard symbols, and label the proband, affected individuals and obligate carriers.

lessons.title: Autosomal or Sex-Linked, Dominant or Recessive
lessons.objective: Decide from a pedigree whether a trait is autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked recessive or X-linked dominant, and compute the carrier probability for a named individual.

units.title: Mitosis, Meiosis and the Human Karyotype
units.summary: Segregation and independent assortment are not abstractions — they are anaphase I. The karyotype is where a meiotic error becomes something you can count on a page.
objectives: Order the stages of mitosis and meiosis and say what each produces.
Read a human karyotype and attribute an aneuploidy to nondisjunction.

lessons.title: Mitosis, Stage by Stage
lessons.objective: Order prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase and cytokinesis, and state what happens to sister chromatids and the spindle in each.

lessons.title: Meiosis and Where Variation Comes From
lessons.objective: Order the events of meiosis I and meiosis II, and identify the two stages at which crossing over and independent assortment generate gamete variety.

lessons.title: Karyotypes, Nondisjunction and Aneuploidy
lessons.objective: Read a human karyotype for chromosome number, sex chromosomes and banding, and attribute trisomy 21, 45,X or 47,XXY to nondisjunction in meiosis.

units.title: DNA: Structure, Replication and Packaging
units.summary: Directionality does most of the work in this unit: 5' to 3' is why one strand lags, why primers point the way they do, and why a sequencing reaction reads in the direction it does.
objectives: Label a nucleotide, a base pair and the 5' and 3' ends of an antiparallel duplex.
Name the enzymes at a replication fork and say what each one does on the leading and lagging strands.

lessons.title: Nucleotides, Base Pairing and 5' to 3'
lessons.objective: Label the three parts of a nucleotide, pair the bases with the correct hydrogen bond count, and identify the 5' and 3' ends of each strand in an antiparallel duplex.

lessons.title: The Replication Fork and Its Enzymes
lessons.objective: Trace replication from origin to finished strands, naming helicase, primase, DNA polymerase and ligase, and explain why the lagging strand is built as Okazaki fragments.

lessons.title: From Double Helix to Chromosome, and the Plasmid Exception
lessons.objective: Order DNA, nucleosome, chromatin fibre and chromosome by scale, contrast euchromatin with heterochromatin, and say how a plasmid differs from a bacterial chromosome.

units.title: Mutation and Repair
units.summary: Two different questions get asked about the same event: what changed in the DNA, and what that does to the protein. They have different answers, and the second one is where the points are.
objectives: Classify a change as substitution, insertion, deletion, inversion, duplication or translocation.
Predict whether a base change is silent, missense, nonsense or frameshift and give its protein-level effect.

lessons.title: What Changed: Substitutions, Indels and Rearrangements
lessons.objective: Classify a change as a substitution, insertion, deletion, inversion, duplication or translocation from a before-and-after sequence or karyotype.

lessons.title: Silent, Missense, Nonsense, Frameshift
lessons.objective: Given a base change and a codon table, decide whether it is silent, missense, nonsense or frameshift and state the effect on the polypeptide.

lessons.title: UV Damage and Nucleotide Excision Repair
lessons.objective: Explain how UVB produces a pyrimidine dimer and how nucleotide excision repair removes it, using xeroderma pigmentosum as the failure case.

units.title: The Central Dogma
units.summary: One sequence, three readings: the template strand, the mature mRNA and the polypeptide. Most molecular questions are asking you to convert between them without losing directionality.
objectives: Convert a DNA template into pre-mRNA, mature mRNA and an amino acid sequence.
Name the parts and steps of transcription, RNA processing and translation in order.

lessons.title: DNA to RNA to Protein
lessons.objective: State the central dogma, say which molecule carries information at each step, and identify where the exceptions to it sit.

lessons.title: Transcription: Promoter to Terminator
lessons.objective: Walk RNA polymerase from promoter recognition through elongation to termination, naming the template and coding strands and the terminator.

lessons.title: Splicing, Capping and the Poly(A) Tail
lessons.objective: Convert a pre-mRNA to a mature mRNA by removing introns, joining exons and adding the 5' cap and poly(A) tail.

lessons.title: Translation at the Ribosome
lessons.objective: Translate an mRNA sequence into amino acids with a codon table, naming the start codon, anticodon pairing, peptide bond formation and the release factor that ends it.

units.title: Gene Regulation and the Operons
units.summary: The lac and trp operons are worth learning as opposites: one is switched on by the sugar it digests, the other switched off by the amino acid it builds.
objectives: Distinguish an activator from a repressor by what it binds and what it does to transcription.
Predict the transcription state of the lac and trp operons from the nutrients present.

lessons.title: Activators, Repressors and the Operator
lessons.objective: Distinguish an activator from a repressor by its binding site and its effect on transcription rate.

lessons.title: The lac Operon
lessons.objective: Predict whether the lac operon is transcribed for a given combination of lactose and glucose, naming allolactose, the lac repressor and catabolite repression.

lessons.title: The trp Operon and Attenuation
lessons.objective: Explain how tryptophan switches the trp operon off, both through the corepressor and through attenuation at the leader sequence.

units.title: Populations, Frequencies and Continuous Traits
units.summary: The scale changes from a family to a population, and so does the arithmetic: two equations, five assumptions, and a short list of named ways those assumptions fail.
objectives: Compute allele and genotype frequencies under Hardy–Weinberg from one observed frequency.
Attribute a change in allele frequency to drift, founder effect, bottleneck, migration or unequal fitness.

lessons.title: Working the Hardy–Weinberg Equations
lessons.objective: Given one genotype frequency in a population, compute p, q and the two remaining genotype frequencies.

lessons.title: The Five Assumptions and What Breaks Them
lessons.objective: Name the Hardy–Weinberg assumptions and identify which one a described population violates.

lessons.title: Drift, Founder Effect, Bottleneck, Migration and Fitness
lessons.objective: Distinguish genetic drift, founder effect, bottleneck and migration as causes of allele-frequency change, and compute relative fitness from survival or reproduction counts.

lessons.title: Additive Alleles and Continuous Variation
lessons.objective: Explain how additive alleles at several loci produce a continuous, bell-shaped distribution, and separate genetic from environmental contributions to a trait such as height or skin colour.

units.title: PCR and Sequencing
units.summary: Two bench methods built from the replication machinery of an earlier unit: one copies a region until there is enough of it, the other stops copies deliberately to read the sequence off.
objectives: Give the temperature and purpose of each PCR step and the role of each component.
Explain how chain termination makes a Sanger reaction readable, and how it differs from ordinary PCR.

lessons.title: PCR: Denature, Anneal, Extend
lessons.objective: State the temperature and purpose of denaturation, annealing and extension, name the components of the reaction, and say why copy number grows exponentially with cycles.

lessons.title: Sanger Sequencing and Chain Termination
lessons.objective: Explain how dideoxynucleotides terminate a growing chain, how the fragments are separated and read, and what Sanger sequencing does that ordinary PCR does not.
